# 1 Maccabees Chapter 16 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Verses:** 24 | **Disagreements:** 22

---

## Summary
The final chapter of 1 Maccabees. Disagreements are concentrated in Simon's farewell speech (vv.2-3), the assassination narrative (vv.15-17), and the closing Kings-formula (vv.23-24). PNEUMA's dramatic register diverges most strongly in the assassination scene.

---

## Disagreements

**v.2** — "from our youth until this day" — all four agree.
- "things have prospered in our hands to deliver Israel many times" (EMET) vs. "it has been given to us to deliver Israel many times" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "God has used us to rescue Israel many times" (PNEUMA — adds "God" explicitly) — theologically significant: 1 Maccabees avoids naming God in narrative; PNEUMA's addition is interpretive.

**v.3** — "by his mercy" (EMET) vs. "by God's mercy" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "by God's grace" (PNEUMA)
- "of mature age" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "men of age" (LOGOS) vs. "in your prime" (PNEUMA)
- "let the help from heaven be with you" (EMET) vs. "may help from Heaven be with you" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "May Heaven be on your side" (PNEUMA)

**v.4** — "men of war and cavalry" (EMET) vs. "warriors and cavalry" (LOGOS) vs. "infantry and cavalry" (PNEUMA/SOPHIA) — clarification of the two contingents.

**v.5** — "behold, a great army came to meet them" (EMET) vs. "a large army came to meet them" (LOGOS) vs. "A large enemy force came to meet them" (PNEUMA adds "enemy") vs. "a great army met them" (SOPHIA)
- "a torrent" (EMET) vs. "a stream" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "a stream" (PNEUMA) — Greek: χειμάρρους; "stream" preferred.

**v.6** — "drew near opposite them for battle" (EMET) vs. "drew up facing them for battle" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "brought his men up to the streambank" (PNEUMA)
- "the people were afraid to cross the torrent" (EMET) vs. "his men were afraid to cross the stream" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA)
- "he crossed first, and the men saw it and crossed after him" — all agree; a classic leadership moment.

**v.7** — "put the cavalry in the midst of the infantry" — all agree.

**v.8** — "many of his men fell wounded" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "many of his men fell" (LOGOS) vs. "his men went down in heaps" (PNEUMA)

**v.9** — "Judas the brother of John was wounded" — all agree.
- "until he came to Kidron which Cendebaeus had built" — all agree.

**v.10** — "the towers that were in the fields of Azotus" (EMET) vs. "the towers in the fields of Azotus" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "the towers around Azotus" (PNEUMA)
- "about two thousand of them fell" — all agree.

**v.11** — "had been appointed commander over the plain of Jericho" — all agree.
- "he had much silver and gold" (EMET) vs. "he had accumulated much silver and gold" (LOGOS/SOPHIA)

**v.13** — "his heart was lifted up" (EMET) vs. "his heart grew proud" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "Power and money inflated him" (PNEUMA paraphrase)
- "purposed to get possession of the country" (EMET) vs. "determined to make himself master of the country" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "dreaming of seizing the whole country" (PNEUMA)
- "dealt treacherously with Simon and his sons to destroy them" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "devised a treacherous plan to do away with Simon and his sons" (LOGOS) vs. "laid a trap for Simon and his sons" (PNEUMA)

**v.14** — PNEUMA converts regnal year to "134 BCE"; others preserve regnal year.
- "the month of Shebat" — all four preserve the Hebrew month name; the only Hebrew month name in the book.

**v.15** — "received them with treachery" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "received them...with treachery" (LOGOS) vs. "received them at a small fort" (PNEUMA — relocates "treachery" to the setup sentence)
- "a little stronghold" (EMET) vs. "a small stronghold" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA)

**v.16** — "had become drunk with wine" (EMET) vs. "had drunk deeply" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "had drunk themselves into a stupor" (PNEUMA)
- "came upon Simon in the banquet hall" (EMET) vs. "rushed upon Simon in the banqueting hall" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "burst into the dining room" (PNEUMA)
- "killed him and his two sons and some of his servants" — all four agree.

**v.17** — "he committed a great act of treachery and returned evil for good" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "he committed a great act of treachery and repaid good with evil" (LOGOS) vs. "he repaid every good Simon had done him with murder" (PNEUMA)

**v.18** — "wrote these things and sent to the king" (EMET) vs. "wrote an account of all this and sent it to the king" (LOGOS/SOPHIA)
- "that he should give over to him their country and their cities" (EMET) vs. "to hand over to him the country and the cities" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA)

**v.21** — "someone ran ahead and reported to John" (EMET) vs. "someone ran ahead and told John" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "a man ran ahead of them and got to John first" (PNEUMA — clarifies he outran the assassins)
- "his father and his brothers had perished" (EMET) vs. "his father and brothers had been killed" (LOGOS) vs. "his father is dead. Your brothers are dead." (PNEUMA dramatizes as direct speech) vs. "his father and brothers had perished" (SOPHIA)

**v.22** — "he was greatly shocked" (EMET) vs. "he was greatly shaken" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "the news hit John like a blow" (PNEUMA)
- "he seized the men who came to kill him and killed them" (EMET) vs. "he seized the men...and put them to death" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "seized the would-be assassins...and had them executed" (PNEUMA)

**v.23-24** — The closing Kings formula: all four translators recognize the deliberate echo of the Deuteronomistic History's regnal summary formulas.
- "the annals of his high priesthood" (EMET/LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "the record book of his high priesthood" (PNEUMA) — "annals" preferred by three translators; this is the book's final phrase.
- "from the time when he became high priest after his father" (EMET) vs. "from the time he succeeded his father as high priest" (LOGOS) vs. "from the day he succeeded his father" (PNEUMA) vs. "from the time he became high priest after his father" (SOPHIA)

---

## Note on the Ending

The book ends mid-sentence in history: Ptolemy has seized Dok, killed Simon, sent assassins after John, and dispatched forces toward Jerusalem — and the narrative simply stops. John Hyrcanus (the "John" of this chapter) went on to reign for thirty years as high priest and ethnarch, but the author is silent about it. The "annals of his high priesthood" — a document never recovered — is cited as the source for his story. This abrupt ending mirrors 2 Kings 24-25 and mirrors the literary strategy of ending the Maccabees cycle before the dynasty becomes morally compromised. SOPHIA notes this literary intentionality in closing.
